The public work index clearly presents composed, labelled monochrome imagery at rest. Direct hover/leave observation shows colour is intentionally removed and restored, while the successful JPEG response and stable intrinsic dimensions distinguish the still from loading, placeholder, or broken-image states.

The entry cluster uses the red-warmed near-black ground and pale green-warmed ink, while both the work index and roster reverse that exact shared pair. Screenshots confirm the visual relationship across all three required surfaces, and measured styles plus the shared CSS variables establish that the grounds are deliberately chromatic rather than neutral black/white or unrelated temperatures.

Both desktop and narrow-window states show the required name, label, mark, and portrait as a single, centered roster composition under the dominant name. Direct bounding boxes and the delivered grid/alignment rules confirm the shared axis and controlled spacing; surrounding controls are much smaller and peripheral, so the name does not share the screen’s weight.

Keyboard testing directly exercised controls on the pale and dark themes and photographic controls. In every required context the focused control was visually findable, using an intentional, theme-adaptive 2px solid ring with spacing from the control rather than an unstyled browser-default indicator. This verifies the requested surfaces without claiming broader WCAG conformance.

The narrow breakpoint is recognizably the same interactive roster: identical talent set and traversal order, identical single-active-talent model, and the same name/discipline/portrait/profile/counter composition. It does not turn into a page structure absent from the wide layout.

Although the reel canvas is procedurally driven by its media row seed and the main still gradient is seed-driven, the binary-file and still-grain violations conclusively make this conjunctive criterion false.

Direct inspection of the complete delivered source establishes one naming form on each relevant surface: lowercase snake_case modules, plural lowercase snake_case tables (with no domain model layer), lowercase snake_case template files, and lowercase snake_case template context keys. Both direct behavior and source prove that uppercase `Rives` and lowercase `rives` diverge because read paths do not use the central slug normalizer. UTC instant handling appears consistent, but the failed slug convention is sufficient to make R28 false.
